title: Strategy as a theory of change
authors: Sergio G. Lazzarini; Todd R. Zenger; Teppo Felin
affiliations: Insper São Paulo Brazil; David Eccles School of Business University of Utah Salt Lake City Utah USA
abstract: Abstract Research Summary The theory‐based view argues that a strategist's task is to develop a theory to move the organization to an improved future state. Focusing on theorizing as a thought process of model creation, we propose a framework to specify hypothetical causal links and analyze their structure as a directed graph connecting inputs, activities, and indicators of problem resolution. We then propose a set of metrics operationalizing key theory attributes: complexity, equifinality, interdependence, and circularity. We discuss the strategic relevance of these attributes in terms of a theory's ability to promote comprehensive problem resolution as well as implement, evaluate, and replicate the proposed solution. Our work represents a step toward operationalizing model creation in the theory‐based view and informs the design of strategic theories of change. Managerial Summary Strategists often theorize how to move their organizations toward an improved performance state. Yet most strategic analysis tools describe the organization's external environment or the internal components of its business model, without precisely specifying forward‐looking interventions that might cause the desired changes. In this paper, we represent strategic theories as a chain of causal interventions—inputs and activities that address relevant problems and lead to desirable outcomes. We propose a structured framework that helps managers develop theories and measure key attributes that influence comprehensive problem resolution and the ability to implement, evaluate, and replicate the proposed interventions. In this sense, our work helps managers mentally create their strategic theories and assess their usefulness as a roadmap to superior performance.

title:
Materiality and investor reaction to environmental
                    <scp>corporate social responsibility</scp>
                    : A replication and extension of Flammer (2013)
authors: Steven D. Kofford; Ben W. Lewis; Myles Melancon
affiliations: Department of Management, College of Business Colorado State University Fort Collins Colorado USA; Department of Management, Marriott School of Business Brigham Young University Provo Utah USA; School of Business Mississippi Christian University Clinton Mississippi USA
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We replicate and extend Flammer's (2013) event study of investor reaction to environmental corporate social responsibility. Flammer found that investors react positively to eco‐friendly events and negatively to eco‐harmful events, with positive reactions diminishing and negative reactions intensifying from 1980 to 2009. We confirm her results in a narrow replication and find that these time trends persist in a quasi‐replication extending the sample through 2019, despite major shifts in the institutional environment for sustainability investing. We then extend Flammer by incorporating financial materiality and find that the investor reactions and time trends Flammer observed are primarily concentrated in material events. Notably, investors drew this distinction throughout the 40‐year window we study, predating the institutionalization of materiality‐based sustainability analysis. Managerial Summary We examine how investors respond to companies' environmental actions. Analyzing 40 years of data on US‐listed public firms, we find that investors reward companies for eco‐friendly actions and penalize them for harmful ones. Over time, these reactions have shifted: investors have grown less enthusiastic about eco‐friendly actions and more critical of harmful ones. Importantly, investors react primarily to environmental actions that are financially relevant, or “material,” to the business and were doing so well before formal standards existed. Within material actions, positive reactions to eco‐friendly initiatives have weakened while negative reactions to eco‐harmful ones have grown stronger. These findings suggest that managers should prioritize environmental initiatives closely tied to their company's financial performance.

title: Who Benefits from Citizenship? Varying Effects of Naturalization Decisions in the Early-Twentieth-Century United States
authors: Peter Catron; Nathan I. Hoffmann; Mingze Li
affiliations: University of Washington, USA; Emory University, USA
abstract: Citizenship acquisition is widely viewed as a mechanism for improving economic outcomes, yet little is known about whether its benefits are distributed evenly. This article examines the varied returns to naturalization in the early-twentieth-century United States, assessing whether naturalization uniformly benefits all immigrants or is especially impactful for those already positioned to profit. Using naturalization records from New York City’s Southern District in the early 1900s, we construct a novel historical dataset for 1,947 immigrants who declared their intent to naturalize. By linking these records to U.S. census data from 1920, 1930, and 1940, we are able to observe immigrants’ characteristics at the point when they make naturalization decisions and to track their outcomes over time. Our findings reveal that immigrants who completed the naturalization process attained significantly higher occupational status than those who initiated but did not complete naturalization. In addition, citizenship is most transformative for those facing the greatest disadvantages. Additional analyses corroborate these findings in linked full-count census data for the entire United States. Citizenship confers occupational advantages not only through formal rights but as a resource that enables claims-making in the labor market, with greater returns to less advantaged immigrants.

title: Demand for Research and the Composition of Scientific Response: Intellectual Distance, Research Productivity, and Research Outcomes
authors: Jino Lu
affiliations: Washington University in St Louis, Olin Business School, St. Louis, Missouri, United States
abstract: When demand for research in a domain increases, scientific progress depends not only on whether more research is produced, but also on which scientists produce that research. This distinction is especially important in emerging domains, where technological trajectories remain uncertain and progress often requires the generation and integration of heterogeneous scientific knowledge. This study examines how academic scientists respond when demand for research increases in a domain and what research outcomes they produce within that domain. Empirically, I exploit the Zero Emission Vehicle (ZEV) mandate, which led to an unanticipated increase in demand for electric vehicle (EV) research. I find that scientists became more likely to produce EV research after the mandate. However, this response varied systematically across scientists: as intellectual distance from the EV domain increased, more-productive scientists were less responsive than less-productive scientists. Yet among scientists who produced EV research, the research outcomes of scientists from more distant domains were associated with greater novelty, while those of more-productive scientists from more distant domains were associated with greater scientific impact and greater use in downstream EV inventions. These findings suggest that increased demand for research shapes not only the volume of scientific activity in a domain, but also the composition of scientists who produce that research.

title: Impact of Data Privacy Regulations on Recommender Systems Performance
authors: Liben Chen; Meizi Zhou; Yicheng Song; Gediminas Adomavicius
affiliations: University of Minnesota, Information and Decision Sciences, Minneapolis, Minnesota, United States; Boston University, Information Systems, Boston, Massachusetts, United States; university of minnesota, carlson school of management, minneapolis, Minnesota, United States
abstract: Data privacy regulations empower consumers to control the collection of their personal data. A significant consequence of these regulations is their effect on various data-driven business solutions, especially on personalization technologies and recommender systems. We investigate the potential impacts of diverse real-world data privacy practices (that can be adopted by firms in response to various data protection regulations) on the recommender systems performance. We also examine how these impacts vary across different personalization contexts and applications. In particular, we distinguish between scenarios where the user population exhibits more stable vs. more dynamic (i.e., changing) preferences, as these scenarios often represent distinctly different recommendation settings. We use a simulation framework, carefully seeded with real-world data, for a comprehensive evaluation of the recommender system performance under numerous scenarios, such as different recommendation algorithms, different data privacy practices, different degrees of users' preference dynamics, etc. Extensive computational experiments uncover several robust performance patterns for different data privacy practices and highlight substantial differences between recommendation settings with stable vs. changing user preferences. Furthermore, building upon the comprehensive findings from our computational experiments, we propose flexible, parameterizable data privacy practice designs based on the notion of revelation protection. The proposed approach is designed to provide an effective balance between personalization performance and privacy considerations, as demonstrated using extensive simulation experiments. The findings of this study have significant implications for the design of privacy-aware recommender systems in the context of contemporary data protection regulations. The findings can also be informative to policymakers for understanding the practical implications of various data privacy practices and for designing future policies.

title: Leveraging social legitimacy to navigate geopolitical fragmentation and populist polarization
authors: Izzet Sidki Darendeli; TL Hill
abstract: Abstract Although earning political legitimacy helps MNEs manage political risk, association with governments and political elites can become liabilities when regimes, alliances, and public sentiment shift. Reflecting on our study of MNE survival during abrupt regime change, we revisit social legitimacy as a complement to, and sometimes a substitute for, political legitimacy. We distinguish two foundations of social legitimacy: relational legitimacy, built through broad ties across societal constituencies, and material legitimacy, earned by providing products, services, and investments perceived as valuable by non-elite society. Although long recognized as a part of earning and maintaining a license to operate in any country, social legitimacy has become an increasingly important hedge against the ebbs and flows of political power driven by geopolitical fragmentation, populism, and polarization. Indeed, as geopolitics and populism make political affiliations more noticeable and more volatile, we suggest that efforts to earn social legitimacy play an increasingly important role in MNE nonmarket strategy. We identify theoretical and empirical questions concerning the sources, usefulness, and limits of earning social legitimacy; urge researchers and leaders to learn from and connect to non-elite sectors of society; and suggest ways that investment in social legitimacy can help MNEs navigate political turbulence worldwide.

title: A Moral Foundations Perspective on CEO Political Ideology
authors: Moritz Appels; Marc Kowalzick; Michael Woywode
affiliations: Erasmus University Rotterdam; University of Mannheim
abstract: As a reflection of their fundamental value systems, CEOs’ political ideology has come to be regarded as a major predictor of their strategic decision-making. Among the most persistent characterizations in this literature, liberal-leaning CEOs are considered to exhibit a distinct preference for evenhanded outcomes and pro-social corporate practices due to their ideological endorsement of equality—an association derived from the conceptualization of political ideologies along the motivated cognition perspective and routinely used to differentiate them from their more conservative peers. Yet, moral psychologists increasingly call for a broader understanding of the moral values differentiating liberals and conservatives. We therefore introduce moral foundations theory to the study of CEO political ideology, according to which liberal- and conservative-leaning CEOs differ in their focus on individual- versus group-centric concerns but, contrary to the existing consensus, should both endorse evenhanded outcomes and pro-social corporate practices. We find evidence for corresponding U-shaped rather than linear effects of CEOs’ political ideology in a sample of over 1,600 S&P 1500 CEOs. As such, we offer a novel theoretical perspective on CEOs’ political ideology and its organizational ramifications.

title: Competitive Dormancy in Interfirm Rivalry: Consequences for Rival Actions
authors: Tianxu Chen; Jianhong Chen; Lingling Pan; Wenpin Tsai; Ming-Jer Chen
affiliations: West Virginia University; University of New Hampshire; University of Pittsburgh; Pennsylvania State University; University of Virginia
abstract: In this study, we examine the implications of competitive dormancy, defined as a situation in which a focal firm’s observed time span of inaction following its prior action has exceeded the firm’s typical duration between successive actions. We argue that competitive dormancy may be perceived as inconsistent with a rival’s expectations and may be associated with an interpretive process concerning the rival’s subsequent actions. Integrating expectancy violation theory (EVT) and competitive dynamics research, we propose that the relationship between a focal firm’s competitive dormancy and the likelihood of rivals’ subsequent actions varies with their relative market standing and strategic resource commitment. Using a sample of 78,055 daily observations from 28 firms across 14 industries from 2000 to 2017, we find support for our hypotheses.

title: The Effects of School Phone Bans: National Evidence from Lockable Pouches
authors: Hunt Allcott; Jason Baron; Thomas Dee; Angela L Duckworth; Matthew Gentzkow; Brian Jacob
affiliations: Stanford University and NBER; Duke University and NBER; University of Pennsylvania; University of Michigan and NBER
abstract: Abstract Schools across the U.S. have sharply restricted student use of phones during the school day. We evaluate one type of restriction—lockable phone pouches—using nationwide data combining a large-scale teacher survey, GPS pings, standardized test scores, and school administrative records, along with sales records from the largest pouch provider. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design, we find that pouch adoption substantially reduces phone use as measured by GPS pings and teacher reports. In the first year after adoption, disciplinary incidents increase, and we find suggestive evidence that student subjective well-being falls, consistent with short-term disruption. However, disciplinary effects fade, while the estimated effects on well-being appear to recover and become positive in later years. For academic achievement, average effects on test scores are consistently close to zero. High schools see modest positive effects, particularly in math, while middle schools see small negative effects. We find little evidence of effects on school attendance and no clear evidence of improvements in self-reported classroom attention or perceived online bullying.

title: Front Matter
The Unequal Economic Consequences of Carbon Pricing
authors: Diego R. Känzig
affiliations: Northwestern University, CEPR, and NBER (email: )
abstract: This paper studies the economic impacts of carbon pricing. Exploiting institutional features of the European carbon market and high-frequency data, I identify carbon policy shocks and trace their dynamic effects. A restrictive carbon policy shock raises energy prices, reduces emissions, spurs green innovation, but decreases economic activity—disproportionately burdening poorer households. Not only are the poor more affected because of their higher energy spending, but they also experience larger income losses. These indirect, general equilibrium effects via income and employment play an important role in the transmission of carbon pricing policies, accounting for about two-thirds of the aggregate consumption response. (JEL E23, E24, O44, Q41, Q54, Q55, Q58)

title: Reproducible Aggregation of Sample-Split Statistics
authors: David M. Ritzwoller; Joseph P. Romano
affiliations: Stanford University (email: )
abstract: Statistical inference is often simplified by sample splitting. This simplification comes at the cost of the introduction of randomness not native to the data. We propose a simple procedure for sequentially aggregating statistics constructed with multiple splits of the same sample. The user specifies a bound and a nominal error rate. If the procedure is implemented twice on the same data, the nominal error rate approximates the chance that the results differ by more than the bound. We illustrate the application of the procedure to several widely applied econometric methods. (JEL C20, C30, C52)

title: The Returns to Government R&D: Evidence from US Appropriations Shocks
authors: Andrew J. Fieldhouse; Karel Mertens
affiliations: Mays Business School, Texas A&M University (email: ); Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas, CEPR (email: )
abstract: Based on a narrative classification of all significant postwar changes in R&D appropriations for five major federal agencies, we find that an increase in nondefense R&D appropriations leads to increases in various measures of innovative activity and higher business-sector productivity in the long run. We structurally estimate the production function elasticity of nondefense government R&D capital using the SP-IV methodology of Lewis and Mertens (2024) and obtain implied returns of 140 to 210 percent over the postwar period. The estimates indicate that government-funded R&D accounts for one-fifth of business-sector TFP growth since WWII and imply substantial underfunding of nondefense R&D. (JEL D24, E23, H50, O31, O33, O38)

title: Residential Segregation and Unequal Access to Local Public Services in India: Evidence from 1.5 Million Neighborhoods
authors: Sam Asher; Kritarth Jha; Paul Novosad; Anjali Adukia; Brandon Tan
affiliations: Imperial College London (email: ); Development Data Lab (email: ); Dartmouth College (email: )
abstract: We study residential segregation and access to public services across 1.5 million urban and rural neighborhoods in India. Muslim and Scheduled Caste segregation in India is high by global standards and only slightly lower than Black-White segregation in the United States. Within cities, public facilities and infrastructure are systematically less available in Muslim and Scheduled Caste neighborhoods. Nearly all regressive allocation is across neighborhoods within cities—at the most informal and least studied form of government. These inequalities are not visible in the aggregate data typically used for research and policy. (JEL H76, J15, O15, O17, O18, R23)

title: Durables and the Marginal Propensity to Spend
authors: Nathan Zorzi; Martin Beraja
affiliations: Dartmouth (email: ); UC Berkeley and NBER (email: )
abstract: Durables represent a large share of households' marginal propensity to spend (MPX). We develop a quantitative model of spending that takes durables into account and matches a rich set of empirical regularities simultaneously. Scaling the response of nondurables provides a poor approximation of the MPX on durables when it comes to its distribution in the population, its persistence over time, and its cyclicality. As an application, we study how the MPX varies with the size of stimulus checks and find that it declines more slowly compared to a model of purely nondurable spending. (JEL D11, E21, E32, E62, G51)

title: Union Bargaining Power and the Amenity-Wage Trade-Off
authors: Lorenzo Lagos
affiliations: Brown University, NBER, and IZA (email: )
abstract: This paper studies how collective bargaining affects wages and amenities. By merging collective bargaining agreements (CBAs) to linked employer-employee data in Brazil, I combine rich contracted amenities with wage information. I implement a difference-in-differences strategy that exploits a court ruling enforcing CBA continuation (i.e., ultra-activity) to estimate the effects of union bargaining power. Strengthening unions raises wages and amenities without reducing employment—increasing retention despite some labor-labor substitution. A revealed-preference approach shows that amenities account for 45 percent of total compensation gains. These findings suggest that collective bargaining can offset monopsony power, but employers retain the right-to-manage workforce composition. (JEL J31, J32, J42, J51, J52, O15)

title: Firm Adaptation in Production Networks: Evidence from Extreme Weather Events in Pakistan
authors: Clare Balboni; Johannes Boehm; Mazhar Waseem
affiliations: London School of Economics and Political Science (email: ); University of Geneva (email: )
abstract: This paper considers how far private adaptation may reduce future vulnerability to climate risks. Using data on monthly firm-to-firm transactions from Pakistan, we find that flood-affected firms are more likely to relocate to safer ground and shift purchases toward suppliers in less flood-prone regions and reached via less flood-prone roads. The results indicate that firms are imperfectly informed about flood risk and update their beliefs following floods. We quantify aggregate impacts using a spatial model of endogenous production network formation. The findings suggest that firms' learning will shape the economic impact of increasingly frequent climate-related disasters. (JEL D22, L14, O13, O14, Q54, R32)

title: Inequality and Racial Backlash: Evidence from the Reconstruction Era and the Freedmen's Bureau
authors: Eric Chyn; Kareem Haggag; Bryan A. Stuart
affiliations: Department of Economics, University of Texas-Austin, and NBER (email: ); Anderson School of Management, University of California-Los Angeles, and NBER (email: ); Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia and IZA (email: )
abstract: How do majority groups respond to narrowing inequality in racially polarized environments? We study this by examining the Freedmen's Bureau, an agency created after the US Civil War to aid former slaves and launch institutional reform in the South. Using new historical records and an event-study approach, we estimate the bureau's impact on political, social, and economic outcomes. Vote shares for Democrats, the party that previously championed slavery and opposed Black civil rights, initially eroded in bureau counties, but these impacts faded as federal oversight weakened. Racial backlash emerged rapidly and persisted, suggesting White majorities sought to offset Black progress. (JEL D63, D72, J15, N31, N41)

title: The Inflation Attention Threshold and Inflation Surges
authors: Oliver Pfäuti
affiliations: The University of Texas at Austin (email: )
abstract: The recent inflation surge brought inflation back on people's minds. I quantify when and how much attention to inflation changes and derive the macroeconomic implications of these attention changes. I estimate an attention threshold at an inflation rate of 4 percent, that attention doubles when inflation exceeds this threshold, and that supply shocks have stronger and more persistent effects on inflation in times of high attention. Developing a model featuring the attention threshold, I show that attention changes offer a joint explanation for inflation surges, inflation's co-movement with inflation expectations, and a long last mile of disinflation. (JEL D84, E12, E31, E43, E52)

title: The Causal Effects of Global Supply Chain Disruptions on Macroeconomic Outcomes: Evidence and Theory
authors: Xiwen Bai; Jesús Fernández-Villaverde; Yiliang Li; Francesco Zanetti
affiliations: Tsinghua University (email: ); University of Pennsylvania (email: ); Peking University HSBC Business School and UIBE (email: ); University of Oxford (email: )
abstract: We study the causal effects of global supply chain disruptions by constructing a new index of real-time port congestion using Automatic Identification System data from container ships and a spatial clustering algorithm. We develop a model with search frictions between producers and retailers that links upstream production slack to downstream supply shortages and captures output and price responses to supply chain shocks. The co-movements of output, prices, spare capacity, and market tightness provide novel identification restrictions. We find that demand and supply shocks drove US disinflation in 2020, while the inflation surge in 2021 was driven mainly by supply chain shocks. (JEL C43, E31, F14, F23, L14, L92)

title: How peers influence headquarter attention to foreign subsidiaries
authors: Mayank Sewak; Anna Lamin
affiliations: Newcastle University Business School Newcastle upon Tyne UK; Northeastern University Boston Massachusetts USA
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We examine how attention to foreign subsidiaries is structured by peer‐based cues originating both outside and inside the firm. Using the cognitive pillar of the attention‐based view, we show how executives rely on peer reference groups to allocate attention across subsidiaries, and we compare the relative influence of different peer types. Among peers outside the firm, industry peers exert a stronger influence on headquarter attention than home‐country peers, highlighting the dominance of competitive comparability. We also show that attention diffuses within the multinational enterprise, with attention to one subsidiary spilling over to other subsidiaries within the same cognitive category. Also, regional groupings drive stronger attentional spillovers than externally constructed categories. These findings reveal a category‐based process through which headquarter attention is allocated during ongoing foreign operations. Managerial Summary We examine how peer activity shapes where multinational headquarters focus their attention during foreign operations. Rather than monitoring every foreign subsidiary equally, headquarters rely on cues from peers to decide where to look more closely, but not all peer cues are equally influential. Among peers outside the firm, industry competitors have a stronger pull on headquarter attention than firms from the same home country, meaning competitive dynamics matter more than home‐country familiarity in directing headquarter attention. Within the firm, geographic regional groupings shape attention more powerfully than broad market categorizations. When attention is directed toward one subsidiary, it spills over to other subsidiaries in the same grouping, amplifying their visibility. Managers can anticipate where attention flows by understanding which peer categories headquarters finds most compelling.

title: Anticipating Surprises by Expanding a Risk Assessment's Possibility Space Into the Unknown With C – K Theory
authors: James Derbyshire
affiliations: Chester Business School University of Chester, Queen's Park Campus Chester UK
abstract: ABSTRACT What should a risk assessor do if she suspects the possibilities derivable from presently available knowledge are incomplete? Risk analysts often encounter this problem when assessing risk in open systems that produce novel outcomes leading to surprises. The solution is to expand the possibility space into the unknown. Yet the novel possibilities then included cannot be mere figments of the imagination; they must be tethered to presently available knowledge to be credible. This may seem paradoxical: to go beyond presently available knowledge by assessing novel possibilities, which, to be credible, must be grounded in presently available knowledge. Yet it is not quite as contradictory as it may first seem. C – K Theory (CKT) was developed to explain how innovators overcome a similar problem when designing a new product. An innovation involves creating something that has novel features. Some of its components may, therefore, not yet exist, and there may even be uncertainty about whether they are technically feasible. This lack of knowledge makes it difficult to determine the innovation's possibility space—a difficulty similar to that faced when assessing risks in open systems. CKT describes how innovators overcome this problem by iteratively moving between a knowledge space comprising established facts and decidable propositions and a conceptual space representing novel, as‐yet‐undecidable propositions. As illustrated herein using the cases of the credit crunch and the 9/11 terrorist attack, CKT can help anticipate surprises by generating, expanding, and integrating the possibility space within the extended ( C , U ) risk‐assessment framework.

title: Natural Is Not Necessarily Safer: A Probabilistic Assessment of Risk–Risk Trade‐Offs Between Cardiovascular and Genotoxic Effects of Food Preservatives
authors: Min‐Pei Ling; Ying‐Hsuan Lee
affiliations: Department of Food Science National Taiwan Ocean University Keelung City Taiwan
abstract: ABSTRACT To extend product shelf life, it is especially important to prevent foods from deteriorating. Apart from the traditional methods of adding salt or sugar in large amounts, other additives, such as food preservatives, can also be applied to achieve the aim of food preservation. This study employs probabilistic risk assessment (PRA) to quantify human health impacts associated with exposure to sodium chloride, sucrose, benzoic acid (BA), and sorbic acid (SA), utilizing cardiovascular disease (CVD) prevalence and micronuclei (MN) induction frequency as dual epidemiological and toxicological endpoints. We evaluated the risks of natural and artificial preservatives in products, such as pickled vegetables, fermented vegetables, candied fruits, and preserved fruits, with the same antibacterial efficiency and under controlled pH and water activity conditions. The results revealed a significant risk trade‐off: Although the CVD prevalence associated with natural preservatives reached 16.2%–18.2% across different food categories, the MN frequency induced by artificial preservatives remained comparatively lower at 7.4%–11.6%. The results suggest that combining natural and artificial preservatives may reduce sodium chloride or sucrose intake and the associated cardiovascular health risks compared with using natural preservatives alone. These findings indicate that although limiting high‐sodium and high‐sugar foods is crucial for cardiovascular health, dietary exposure to artificial preservatives, such as BA and SA, was associated with relatively low estimated genotoxic risks, though potential hepatic or renal impacts warrant further investigation.

title: Assessing the Relative Contribution of Pre‐Deployment Abroad Versus In‐Mission Dirofilaria immitis Infections in French Military Working Dogs Screened Post‐Mission: A Quantitative Risk Assessment
authors: Amélia Grosbois; Veronica Risco‐Castillo; Stéphanie Watier‐Grillot; Guillaume Crozet
affiliations: Laboratoire de Santé Animale EPIMIM Ecole Nationale Vétérinaire d'Alfort Anses Maisons‐Alfort France; 22e Groupe vétérinaire de Bordeaux Bordeaux France; Laboratoire de Santé Animale, BIPAR Anses, INRAE, Ecole Nationale Vétérinaire d'Alfort Maisons‐Alfort France; Biopôle Alfort Ecole Nationale Vétérinaire d'Alfort Maisons‐Alfort France; Groupe d'experts en épidémiologie animale Direction de la médecine des forces Tours France; Département Anticipation et Intervention Centre d’Épidémiologie et de Santé Publique des Armées Marseille France
abstract: ABSTRACT Dirofilaria immitis ( D. immitis ) is a mosquito‐borne nematode responsible for canine cardiopulmonary dirofilariasis, a parasitic infection widely distributed worldwide and established in mainland France, particularly in southern regions. Military working dogs (MWDs) may be at increased risk of exposure to vector‐borne pathogens because of their predominantly outdoor lifestyle and frequent missions abroad. Nevertheless, D. immitis infection remains sporadic in this population, likely due to well‐implemented medical prophylaxis. The aim of this study was to investigate the likely origin of D. immitis infections detected in MWD during post‐mission screening using a quantitative risk analysis approach. Scenario trees were developed to describe the sequences of events leading to the return of an infected dog from a mission abroad, accounting for parasite biology, prophylactic measures, and compliance. The model estimated a mean annual number of 4.25 infected MWD returning from missions out of an average annual population of 466 returning dogs, of which 79% were detected through post‐mission screening. Most infections were likely acquired before deployment, either during previous missions, at the breeding facility before purchase, or within mainland France. Only 7.9% of infections acquired during missions were expected to be detected by testing performed at the end of the post‐mission quarantine period. Alternative scenarios highlighted the effectiveness of chemoprophylaxis, as its absence was associated with a 3.2‐fold increase in the number of infected dogs. Simulations also showed that extending the interval between return and testing would substantially improve the detection of mission‐acquired infections. These findings support the continued use of preventive measures while questioning the adequacy of current post‐mission screening alone for identifying D. immitis infections acquired during deployment.

title: EXPRESS: Bridging the Gap: The Impact of Online Booking of Healthcare Appointments Service
authors: Liuyi He; Jifeng Luo; Panpan Wang; Zhiyan Wu; Han Zhang
abstract: Online healthcare communities (OHCs) play an important role in transforming healthcare delivery. While existing literature has primarily focused on the impact of teleconsultation services on offline demand, the influence of integrating offline access into OHCs on teleconsultation remains largely unexplored. This study addresses the gap by investigating how the integration of offline access into OHCs affects the utilization of teleconsultation services. We leverage a natural experiment in an OHC involving the implementation of the Online Booking of Healthcare Appointments (OBHA) feature, which allows patients to secure in-person visit appointments in the OHC. Using difference-in-differences (DID) models, we find a significant increase in new demand for adopter physicians’ teleconsultation services following the integration of OBHA, without deterioration in service quality. Notably, the increased demand largely comes from patients in remote and underserved areas seeking consultations with high-quality physicians, exhibiting a cascading effect. Furthermore, we find that OBHA adoption extends the geographic reach of physicians’ teleconsultation services and promotes a more equitable distribution of teleconsultation utilization across regions. Our findings indicate that integrating offline access into OHCs not only boosts the utilization of teleconsultation services but also helps reduce health disparities by facilitating access to high-quality resources. This study contributes to the literature on healthcare operations management, healthcare information technology, and health disparities. The insights gleaned from the study also offer practical suggestions to policymakers, OHC operators, physicians, and patients.

title: EXPRESS: Simplifying the Madness of Multiple Entries in March Madness
authors: Jeff Decary; David Bergman; Carlos Cardonha; Jason Imbrogno; Andrea Lodi
abstract: Multi-entry betting pools for single-elimination tournaments create a portfolio-design problem: a participant may submit several brackets whose scores are highly dependent, while payouts are typically concentrated on the best-performing entry. Motivated by March Madness pools, we study the problem of selecting a portfolio of brackets that maximizes the expected maximum score (EMS) across entries. This objective captures the top-heavy nature of such contests without requiring a model of opponents' bracket choices, which is difficult to estimate reliably in a tournament played only once per year. We first establish computational and structural properties of the EMS objective. Exact EMS evaluation is #P-hard in general, although it is polynomial-time computable for any fixed number of entries with an exponent that grows with the portfolio size. For two entries, EMS decomposes into single-entry expected-score terms and an expected absolute score-gap term, making explicit the trade-off between selecting individually strong brackets and diversifying across outcomes. These insights motivate two sample average approximation algorithms: an entry-by-entry method based on marginal EMS contributions and a round-by-round method that exploits the geometrically increasing scoring weights in March Madness by emphasizing late-round diversification. Computational experiments using historical tournament data show that the round-by-round method scales reliably and outperforms direct SAA and an entropy-based benchmark for larger portfolios. In a real high-stakes DraftKings pool from the 2023 tournament, our 100-entry portfolio would have achieved a 2.54% probability of attaining a maximum-scoring entry, with higher expected profit than the portfolios submitted by several elite professional bettors.

title: EXPRESS: Coevolution of Trader Similarity Networks and Follower Dynamics in Social Trading
authors: Ye Liu; Mingwen Yang; Yong Tan
abstract: Social trading platforms have been gaining popularity against traditional brokerages over the past few years. Compared with traders on traditional financial markets, those on social trading platforms often exhibit more similar trading strategies. In this paper, we examine the impact of strategy similarity patterns on traders' popularity. We identify two competing effects of similarity: a substitution effect, whereby traders with similar strategies become interchangeable and compete for followers; and a social proof effect, whereby similarity signals credibility in an environment characterized by high uncertainty and limited verifiable credentials, thereby attracting followers. To empirically examine these effects, we construct a dynamic similarity network and develop a coevolution model that captures the joint evolution of network structure and follower dynamics. Using data from a leading social trading platform, we find that, on average, greater similarity leads to a decline in a trader’s followers over time, indicating that the substitution effect dominates. Importantly, this relationship is heterogeneous. For more established traders, the substitution effect is stronger, such that greater similarity reduces their popularity. In contrast, for less established traders, the social proof effect dominates, and similarity increases their popularity. Using counterfactual simulations, we show that reducing the density of the similarity network and promoting a more balanced distribution of followers can mitigate the negative substitution effect, thereby increasing the total number of followers on the platform and, consequently, the platform revenue. Our study identifies several managerial and operational implications for the social trading platforms.

title: EXPRESS: The Role of Ease-of-Return Experience on Contingent Free Shipping Policies
authors: Ashish Kabra; Wedad J. Elmaghraby; Nitish Jain
abstract: Contingent free shipping (CFS) policies, whereby consumers get free shipping if their orders exceed a certain amount, are commonplace. Such a policy aims to nudge customers to place larger orders by adding additional items and/or buying more expensive items ( order-swelling ). A less desirable possible outcome is that customers pad their orders to avoid paying the shipping fee but later return the opportunistic or impulse-purchase items ( return-swelling ). A retailer designing the CFS policy’s terms—threshold and shipping fee—should balance these competing effects. We study how the retailer's return environment, specifically the ease-of-return experience (EOR) for customers, moderates order-swelling or return-swelling behavior induced by a CFS policy. We collaborate with an online fashion retailer that switched across multiple CFS policies over time and offered home pickup of returns in some markets but not in others. Our difference-in-differences empirical strategy builds on these policy switches and the location-based variation in the EOR. We find that the EOR can considerably impact the relative profit performance of the CFS policies and that it moderates both the order-swelling and the return-swelling responses. Our counterfactual analysis reveals that return-swelling is the key driver of the observed difference in the relative profit performance of CFS policies across the two EOR market types. Our study documents a novel determinant of the financial performance of a CFS policy: the ease-of-return experience. Our analysis indicates that our collaborating retailer would be better off selecting a (relatively) lenient CFS policy in more convenient EOR markets and a (relatively) stringent CFS policy in less convenient EOR markets.

title: EXPRESS: Revitalizing the Grocery Store Experience: An Empirical Study on the Spillover Effects of Experiential Services
authors: Bengü Nur Özdemir; Stanley Frederick W. T. Lim
abstract: Grocery retailers increasingly use experiential services to attract customers to their stores. However, it remains unclear whether these services generate positive spillover effects to core grocery sales or cannibalize existing demand. We provide the first empirical evidence by studying a grocery retailer that introduced a taphouse as its first experiential service and examining the underlying mechanisms. We combine store transaction records with SafeGraph's point-of-interest data and survey data on product attributes. Using a quasi-experimental design, we specify a synthetic difference-in-differences estimator with staggered treatment timings. Our results show significant positive spillover effects. On average, stores that feature a taphouse experienced a 5.97% increase in daily sales volume, a 6.82% rise in sales revenue, a 5.76% increase in transactions, and a 6.18% expansion in product variety compared to stores without a taphouse. Our mechanism analyses suggest that these results are associated with activity through both extensive (newly observed customers) and intensive (greater purchasing activity among existing customers) margins. We find that an average order contains fewer but relatively higher-priced items, leaving average order value statistically unchanged. Newly acquired customers make relatively smaller purchases than existing customers, whose order size does not change significantly following the taphouse introduction. We also find that products complementary to the taphouse and those with a greater propensity for impulse purchasing account for larger shares of grocery sales following taphouse introduction. Finally, nearby competing supermarkets experience reductions in both total visits and unique visitors, suggesting that local competitive substitution may contribute to the observed customer expansion. To assess generalizability, we replicate the analysis with another grocery chain in a different region that introduced a full restaurant and obtain qualitatively similar results. Overall, the findings indicate that adding a taphouse can effectively increase grocery sales volume and revenue. Although high setup costs may deter adoption, our break-even analysis projects recovery in approximately 34 to 39 weeks from grocery-side gross-margin contributions alone, or 27 to 44 weeks when alternative assumptions about taphouse profitability, including operating losses, are incorporated.

title: Interesting and impactful research avenues emerge from teaching operations management
authors: Tyson R. Browning
affiliations: Neeley School of Business, Texas Christian University , , ,
abstract: Purpose This article reflects on how teaching operations management (OM) to graduate students and executives provides a rich source of interesting and impactful OM research avenues. Design/methodology/approach While it is common to hear that the latest research should keep teaching fresh and relevant, this article flips this advice to discuss interesting and impactful OM research topics emerging from the challenges of teaching an MBA core course. Findings This article suggests six avenues for future research that emerged from teaching – how company operations pertain to its strategy, the role of chief operating officer (COO), enterprise processes, process improvement, performance measurement, and automation/artificial intelligence (AI) – and specific research questions within each avenue. Research limitations/implications The proposed research questions are exemplary and not comprehensive. Practical implications Addressing the proposed research questions will lead to interesting, practically relevant and impactful results. Social implications Addressing the proposed research questions will lead to socially relevant and impactful results. Originality/value This article reverses the typical admonition to let research inform teaching, showing how considering the counter-relationship illuminates interesting and impactful research avenues.

title: De-risking from China: how US firms reconfigure sourcing through decoupling, diversification and friendshoring across geopolitical disruptions
authors: Remi Charpin; Martin Cousineau; Di Fan
affiliations: HEC Montreal Department of Logistics and Operations Management, , ,; Business Division, School of Fashion and Textiles, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University , ,
abstract: Purpose We examine whether US firms use three location strategies—decoupling, diversification, and friendshoring—to de-risk their sourcing portfolios. We investigate how the use of these strategies varies across bilateral (2018 US–China trade war), systemic (COVID-19 pandemic) and alliance-based (Russia–Ukraine war) shocks. We also test whether firms operating in high-tech industries de-risk more aggressively. Design/methodology/approach Using Panjiva US seaborne import records, we build firm-year measures of the three strategies for 1,565 US firms over 2011–2024. We then estimate fixed-effects models that interact firm's pre-disruption China exposure with the three disruption periods and a high-tech indicator. Findings Highly China-exposed firms decouple during all three disruptions, with decoupling switching on sharply at the trade war. Diversification activates specifically at the COVID-19 pandemic. Friendshoring peaks during the COVID-19 pandemic and reverses once the war begins. Sourcing portfolios appear more diversified and politically aligned, but these gains vanish once the China sourcing share is excluded, revealing them as mechanical by-products of decoupling. High-tech firms generally do not de-risk more than their peers. Originality/value We move the study of de-risking from perception-based case evidence to large-scale observed sourcing behavior. We conceptualize decoupling, diversification, and friendshoring as three sourcing location strategies and match each to its most salient disruption type, laying the groundwork for a contingency theory of strategy–shock fit. We further show that portfolio-wide indices of diversification and political alignment may overstate genuine de-risking because they incorporate the effects of decoupling. Moreover, policymakers' ambitions to de-risk high-tech industries and promote friendshoring have generated only a limited corporate response.

title: When technologies transform: a consideration of open innovation's contributions to operations management
authors: Henry Chesbrough; Yixuan Shi
affiliations: University of California Berkeley , , ,; LUISS University , ,; Aston University , ,
abstract: Purpose This paper examines what an open innovation (OI) perspective contributes to operations and supply chain management when a technology transition reshapes an industry. Earlier operations management research implicitly defined OI as a small set of isolated practices. This paper recovers its fuller depth as bidirectional knowledge flows and a mindset anchored in the business model. Design/methodology/approach The study traces innovation in the global automotive industry across three phases, then develops illustrative case studies of four Chinese electric vehicle (EV) entrants, Kandi, BYD, Xiaomi and Chery, analyzed through outside-in flows, inside-out flows and business model innovation. The cases build on a structured review of Chinese-language academic and industry literature, corroborated against company reports, trade press and industry data. Findings Chinese EVs have attained industry leadership, yet no dominant EV innovation strategy has emerged. All four firms drew heavily, but differently, on external knowledge, much of it from consumer electronics and smartphones, outside the automotive supply chain and each treated the vehicle as a platform. BYD and Chery also pursued inside-out flows, BYD through divisionalization and an open vehicle architecture, Chery through technology exports and internal suppliers. The contribution runs both ways: OI extends operations management research from project-and dyad-level openness to firm-level strategy, while operations management research helps explain organizational configuration and governance in innovation. Research limitations/implications The findings rest on a single industry. Future work should test them in other transforming sectors: pharmaceuticals, financial services and defense. Originality/value The paper reframes OI for operations management scholarship and uses the Chinese EV phenomenon to show how it complements operations management when industry architectures are disrupted.

title: Teaching for Wonder: Pedagogical Openings for Epistemic Change in the Climate Crisis
authors: Chloe Preece; Pilar Rojas‐Gaviria; Emma Surman
affiliations: ESCP Business School 527 Finchley Road London NW3 7BG UK; Kedge Business School 680 Cr de la Libération Talence 33405 France; Birmingham Business School University House, Edgbaston Park Road Birmingham B15 2TY UK
abstract: Abstract The accelerating climate crisis demands profound changes in how management learning and education prepares students to engage with uncertainty and ecological interdependence. While recent scholarship calls for epistemic transformation in business schools, there is limited understanding of how pedagogy might cultivate the orientations required for such change. This paper advances wonder as a critical yet under‐theorized pedagogical orientation for climate‐responsive management education. We conceptualize wonder as an epistemic–affective orientation of attentional widening and humility in response to the more‐than‐known, capable of disrupting instrumental habits of knowing and sustaining openness to uncertainty. Drawing on an interpretive qualitative study of an arts‐based pedagogical collaboration with the Birmingham Royal Ballet, we develop a processual framework comprising five interrelated moments: encounter, suspension, engagement, refiguration and return. Together, these moments show how wonder reshapes students’ relationships to knowledge, enabling them to engage with complexity beyond instrumental frames. In doing so, the paper provides an empirically grounded theorization of wonder as a pedagogical mechanism for epistemic transformation and advances debates on what climate‐responsive management education could look like.

title:
The intelligence loop and value creation in the age of
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    agents
authors: Yong Li; Ming Zeng; Alexis Li
affiliations: Department of Management & Entrepreneurship University of Nevada, Las Vegas Las Vegas Nevada USA; Hupan School of Entrepreneurship Hangzhou Zhejiang China; Brown University Providence Rhode Island USA
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving from generating outputs to executing work. An agent that executes work autonomously produces something generative AI does not: operational experience that can raise its future intelligence. Prior research on AI emphasizes value creation through demand‐side feedback, notably data network effects, in which user data improve prediction and reinforce adoption. We develop the supply‐side counterpart, the intelligence loop: delegated usage generates operational experience, agentic capability converts it into future intelligence, and the resulting value maintains or expands usage. The loop cannot operate until autonomous execution is viable, a threshold we call minimum viable intelligence (MVI). Crossing MVI does not guarantee rising intelligence. Comparable deployments of AI agents can diverge as their loops decay, sustain, or accelerate. Three implications follow. Competitive advantage may depend more on the loop than on installed base. An above‐MVI agent supplies scarce expert skill as a non‐rival, replicable resource, so productive capacity can grow faster than expert headcount, with the one‐person company as a limiting case. And a venture with adequate demand, capital, and a capable team can still fail because its loop never functions or later deteriorates. Managerial Summary Artificial intelligence (AI) agents can execute work, and the experience generated through execution can raise their future intelligence, a feedback process we call the intelligence loop. An agent crosses a workflow's minimum viable intelligence (MVI) when it executes reliably without step‐by‐step direction, autonomous execution creates at least as much net value as the best alternative after oversight and correction costs, and governance arrangements keep residual risk acceptable and accountability clear. Investment belongs where one of these conditions keeps a valuable workflow below MVI. Deployment can begin with narrow, feedback‐rich workflows near MVI that ideally lead to harder workflows, since base model upgrades can match gains on simple work. Even above MVI, the loop is not automatic: it stalls when feedback is not timely and diagnostic, experience yields little intelligence gain, gains add little user value, or value does not maintain or expand usage. Human involvement shifts from executing work to specifying goals, evaluating outputs, governing execution, and supplying tacit knowledge. When the loop sustains or accelerates, productive capacity can grow faster than expert headcount. With capable base models widely available, advantage depends less on access to AI than on building and governing the loop, controlling proprietary operational experience, and converting it into intelligence more effectively than rivals. A venture with adequate demand, capital, and a capable team can fail because its loop never functions or later deteriorates. Cutting evaluation or oversight to scale faster may increase output in the short run but weaken the loop even while revenue remains healthy.

title: Information Aggregation With Delegation of Votes
authors: Amrita Dhillon; Grammateia Kotsialou; Dilip Ravindran; Dimitrios Xefteris
affiliations: King's College London and CIAS Budapest Hungary; King's College London UK; Humboldt University of Berlin Berlin Germany; University of Cyprus Nicosia Cyprus
abstract: ABSTRACT Liquid democracy (LD) combines elements of direct and representative democracy: voters can either vote directly or delegate their votes to others. We study its information aggregation properties in a setting with heterogeneously and privately informed independent and partisan voters. We establish that LD always has equilibria that improve welfare and information aggregation relative to direct democracy, identify economically interpretable conditions under which these gains are strict, and characterise optimal delegation for salient classes of committees. However, while delegation improves the best‐equilibrium, it can also introduce robust inefficient equilibria that perform worse than direct democracy.

title: The Evolution of the Market for Corporate Control
authors: MIKE BURKART; SAMUEL LEE; PAUL VOSS
abstract: ABSTRACT We consider an informed large shareholder who can choose between making a takeover bid herself and initiating a sale to another acquirer. Such takeover activism complements direct takeovers because the very choice mitigates the asymmetric information problem, thereby improving efficiency. As more investors enter the market for corporate control, takeover activism increasingly replaces direct takeovers as the prevailing mode of disciplinary control change, matching the evolution in practice. Our model shows how this evolution, characterized by a symbiotic relationship between investor activism and private equity, arises to overcome asymmetric information and collective action problems through intermediated transactions.

title: Consequences of Fiscal Risk to Optimal Monetary Policy
authors: OTÁVIO DE A. J. TEIXEIRA; VLADIMIR K. TELES
abstract: Abstract We study the optimal monetary policy of a New Keynesian economy on the brink of fiscal dominance. The model features a Markov switching structure to incorporate regime uncertainty. Switching probabilities can be either exogenous or endogenous. We find that a fiscal risk entails a welfare loss and breaks the “divine coincidence” because perfect price stabilization becomes counterproductive when monetary policy affects debt dynamics and agents anticipate regime changes. In this environment, the optimal inflation coefficient in the Taylor rule is decreasing on the fiscal risk, and the optimal regime choice ultimately depends on government credibility.

title: Do Inflation Expectations Improve Model‐Based Inflation Forecasts?
authors: MARTA BAŃBURA; DANILO LEIVA‐LEÓN; JAN‐OLIVER MENZ
abstract: Abstract Those of professional forecasters do. For a wide range of time‐series models for the euro area and its member states, we find a higher average forecast accuracy of models that incorporate information on inflation expectations from the ECB's Survey of Professional Forecasters (SPF) and Consensus Economics compared to their counterparts that do not. The professional forecasters expectations seem to help to correct the upward forecast bias in the low inflation period and to make the model forecasts more robust. By contrast, incorporating expectations derived from financial market prices or those of firms and households does not lead to systematic improvements in forecast performance.

title: Whose Job Is It, Anyway? The Effect of the Review Process on Employee Performance
authors: Adam Bross; Ryan D. Sommerfeldt
affiliations: Auburn University Auburn Alabama USA; Brigham Young University Provo Utah USA
abstract: ABSTRACT Companies have widely adopted a system of work‐product reviews whereby the work of one individual is subsequently reviewed by another to ensure its quality. We examine how managers can effectively implement a review of employee work to improve performance. Organizations review employees' work to identify mistakes and improve work quality. However, reviews may also reduce employees' effort and initiative if they expect reviewers to identify and correct their errors for them. We use an experiment to examine how employee performance depends on who conducts the review and how feedback is provided. Specifically, participants' work was reviewed by either a superior or a peer, and the reviewer provided either general, high‐level guidance (autonomy‐oriented) or specific corrective information about errors (dependency‐oriented). Employees performed best when superiors provided high‐level guidance or when peers provided specific corrective feedback, with these benefits emerging over time. Guidance from a superior increased employees' sense of responsibility, whereas corrective help from a peer strengthened feelings of teamwork and cohesion. Review approaches that did not fit these combinations offered no clear performance benefit relative to having no review. The findings show that review effectiveness depends on matching the feedback approach to the reviewer's organizational rank. These results have important implications for managers, accountants responsible for internal controls, and audit professionals involved in designing and implementing the review process.

title: Mandatory Disclosure and Peer Firms' Learning From Stock Prices
authors: Jaewoo Kim; Hunter Pearson; Brady Twedt
affiliations: Lundquist College of Business University of Oregon Eugene Oregon USA; C. T. Bauer College of Business University of Houston Houston Texas USA; Mays Business School Texas A&M University College Station Texas USA
abstract: ABSTRACT Theory posits that mandatory disclosure influences peer firms' learning from stock prices in two non‐mutually exclusive ways: intra‐industry information transfers and the reallocation of information acquisition efforts. Using mandatory segment disclosure as our setting, we document a decrease in investment‐ q sensitivity for peers of disclosing firms. This effect is stronger among peers with greater economic links to disclosing firms and peers with the greatest incentives to glean information from prices. Our findings provide novel evidence that mandatory disclosure can have significant negative externalities on peer firms' investment efficiency via a managerial learning from the stock price channel. These insights inform regulators assessing the economic consequences of mandatory disclosure, while also assisting managers who rely on information from stock prices to guide investment decisions.

title: Trade Interdependence in the Modern Global Economy
authors: MICHAEL-DAVID MANGINI; STEPHEN CHAUDOIN
affiliations: University of Southern California; Harvard University
abstract: Analyzing global trade interdependence requires an approach that incorporates fundamental features of the modern economy: intense trade in intermediates and the changing availability of alternative partners and substitute products. We use theoretical models of structural gravity to construct measures of dyadic dependence that directly incorporate these features. The measures describe (1) how much trade interruptions damage a country’s welfare and (2) how much additional trade it would take from their existing trade partners to compensate. We then show three important findings. First, the new measures differ from traditional measures based on aggregate trade statistics. Second, they show how, contrary to much common wisdom, the world has not marched inexorably toward greater interdependence. Third, we use China’s foreign assistance, as exemplified by the Belt and Road Initiative, to assess the consequences of one major government policy. Chinese assistance has increased partners’ dependence on China, without a reciprocal increase in Chinese dependence.

title: Councils and Indirect Rule in British Africa
authors: JUTTA BOLT; LEIGH GARDNER; JENNIFER KÖHLER; JACK PAINE; JAMES A. ROBINSON
affiliations: University of Groningen; London School of Economics and Political Science; Emory University; University of Chicago
abstract: Did Western colonial rule transform African political institutions? Despite extensive research on indirect rule, we have little systematic evidence about how colonizers’ aims interacted with the structure of indigenous institutions to shape local governance. We explain why colonizers faced incentives to delegate authority to traditionally legitimate institutions, even in historically decentralized areas. Empirically, we analyze originally compiled data on African political institutions in the precolonial and colonial periods for more than 450 subnational units across British Africa. We focus on councils as a form of executive constraints. Subnational councils were widespread, exhibited strong correlations with precolonial institutions and patterns of socioeconomic development, and exerted meaningful decision-making powers. These indirect-rule institutions reflected reforms to replace ineffective installed agents. Pressure from below prompted British officials to reintroduce systems of executive constraints based on precolonial models. Our findings reject widespread claims that colonizers could unilaterally implement indirect-rule institutions while disregarding precolonial precedents.

title: When Business Speaks, Legislators Listen: Experimental and Qualitative Evidence from Brazil
authors: FERNANDO B. MELLO
affiliations: University Carlos III Madrid
abstract: The influence of interest groups on policy making is a central concern in representative democracies, yet identifying causal effects remains a significant challenge. This article argues that legislators respond to informational cues about the economic importance and coalition breadth of interest groups. A field experiment in Brazil, which randomized the receipt of printed and WhatsApp messages from a pro-reform business organization, reveals that legislators are more likely to vote in favor of the group’s position when its membership size, economic importance, and sectoral reach are emphasized. A survey experiment with lobbyists supports this mechanism, showing that messages highlighting group characteristics increase legislators’ expected engagement and support. In-depth interviews with key political figures—including a former president, ministers, and deputies—further corroborate these findings. This study contributes to the literature on informational lobbying and cue-based persuasion by employing realistic experimental treatments and mixed-methods evidence.

title: Youth Representation and Democratic Legitimacy
authors: Aksel Sundström; Charles T. McClean; Daniel Stockemer
affiliations: University of Gothenburg; Yale University; University of Ottawa
abstract: Abstract How does the age composition of democratic institutions shape public evaluations of their legitimacy? While most institutions are dominated by older politicians, we argue that incorporating younger representatives can enhance perceptions of legitimacy. To test this claim, we conduct a survey experiment in the United States that varies the age composition of a bipartisan state legislative committee and its decisions. We find that including younger members increases perceptions of procedural fairness and institutional trust, and improves evaluations of decisions on lower-salience policies. These effects are stronger among young people and Democrats. Evidence on mechanisms suggests these legitimacy gains reflect beliefs that younger politicians are more attuned to young people’s experiences and concerns. Observational evidence from US state legislatures and a replication experiment in the United Kingdom yield consistent patterns, suggesting that these findings extend beyond the original experimental context. This suggests that expanding youth representation can meaningfully strengthen democratic legitimacy.
